p: Yeah, if the agency could come up with some type of breakdowns of, you know, square miles for this type of bike lane versus that type of bike lane, just something for us to have like some baseline of how this stuff gets priced out, that would be very helpful for us and for members of the public.
Will do.
With this funding, will DOT be able to build out the 50 miles of protected bike lanes of fiscal 27?
So, you know, again, not able to give an exact number yet, but it is a historic level of investment, and therefore, we’re expecting a very substantial increase in the output of bike lane–
[interposing] Compared to years past?
Yes.

And increasing even more in the future years, right? I didn’t mention that earlier, but part of it is of course is once we

get the funding in July, as we hire up, as we expand these contracts, etcetera, all the things it takes to build these, we’re going to do as much as we can this year, but we also expect very significant growth in future years.

I’m going to ask another set of questions– last set of questions before I pass it on and then I’ll come back for more. I have questions on the Knicks and the World Cup. This summer, New York City region will play host to a round of group matches and the final match of the World Cup, and in a few weeks our very own New York Knicks will be playing in the NBA Finals. Has the administration outlined to DOT what their role will be in the upcoming world cup, and what does the scope of the involvement entail?

Thank you, Chair. Yeah, we’re really excited about the World Cup and also about the Knicks– go Knicks– and you know, I think the mayor has said and I agree that the World Cup presents an exciting opportunity not only to show our city off to the world, but to make sure that all New Yorkers benefit from these. So, that’s kind of– I think DOT’s role is two-fold. Number one, we’re

really trying to leverage these events, World Cup in particular, to create opportunities for New Yorkers to celebrate and feel like they’re a part of the World Cup even if they’re not going to see a match in-person. There’s been some announcements around that ad there’s more to come in the coming weeks around watch parties and that kind of stuff. I think also we had the announcement around the Soccer Streets that we’re doing to engage school kids. You know, and then the other side of it is obviously more like the traffic management side, right, I trying to ensure that all this activity doesn’t– that it works smoothly and that we put our best foot forward for visitors, but also that it’s not inconveniencing New Yorkers how all this stuff is happening. And my colleagues could provide more details, but that’s kind of our overall goal.
Over a month ago the Streets Blog reported that there have been watch parties that had been cancelled. Is that true? Or city events that have been scaled down by any chance?

Well, you know, what I’ll say is for myself like coming into this role and realizing that the World Cup was five, six months

away, it’s a lot, and so a lot of these conversations and planning have been happening in a very dynamic real-time way. Multiple agencies are involved and there’s a lot of different pieces. So, everything’s been kind of, you know– it’s been dynamic, but we’re excited with where we’ve landed. We think it’s going to be a wonderful series of activities and events for New Yorkers.
Was the DOT’s decision to scale down events, or is that a different agency?
There was no final set of events that was scaled down. We’ve– it’s, like I said, it’s a lot of conversations and planning that have been happening in real time.
Alright, thank you.

Great. Thank you. Just want to recognize we’ve been joined by Council Members Hanif and Morano on Zoom and also Council Member Brooks-Powers. And just– as we go into member questions, just want to remind colleagues of course if we can keep questions and responses both succinct because we want to make sure we’ll get through everyone, and of course, if any members wants to go

for round two, let us know. And we have– we’re going to start with Council Member Won followed by Council Member Louis.

Thank you so much, Chair Lee. So, I want to break it down a little bit further. So when it comes to a road, an intersection is usually four corners, and you’re repeatedly saying it’s $10,000 for an intersection, but the– then you’re saying that the intersection as a location they’re an eight-part intersection. So, now you’re redefining intersection which we constantly feel like there’s a lot of disagreement on. Then it’s less than $3 billion even with that calculation as well, $3 billion. So, in relation to the mayor campaigning, is there are new– are there new dollars added to this current administration for hardened daylighting, yes or no? Because at the last budget hearing you said that the only daylighting funding that you have is a rollover from the Eric Adams administration.

I mean, I want to start by saying that I apologize if there’s been any miscommunication or misunderstanding around how we’re defining or how we’re laying out the cost. You know, as I mentioned earlier, we’re here in good faith to

work with you to figure out the best pathway forward on daylighting. On cost– you’re asking about cost, Council Member?
Yeah, has new funding been added by the Zohran Mamdani administration–
[interposing] [inaudible]
for daylighting? Because at the last hearing, the only amount of dollars for hardened daylighting was from the Eric Adams administration. Are there new dollars added?

So, there was a tremendous amount of money added to our budget. It’s primarily being called bus lane and bike lane, but as part of a lot of those projects we do include hardening daylighting as part of the safety treatment we bring to the corridor. For example, most of our protected bike lanes include hardened daylighting going down the corridor to make sure that there’s visibility for turning vehicles to be able to see cyclists. So, it’s not called out as a separate line item, but the city is very much committed to and is funding these safety improvements.
So, what is the dollar amount that you're going to set aside for hardened daylighting in your new added budget?

So, just to the point that Deputy Commissioner Beaton was making, there’s no item and we’re not looking at it as one piece. Every time we do a project we’ll make sure if daylighting is an appropriate treatment.

So, then help me understand what specific street design elements are you looking at, and can you help us understand what the criteria is exactly so that we can understand your criteria for your evaluations of which locations you will have hardened daylighting done?

Sure. And I just want to, you know, start by saying that we’re very confident in our ability with the budget that we have now to exceed the prior administration’s level of output of hardened daylighting. As Deputy Commissioner Beaton said, the bike lanes, the bus lanes, all the other Vision Zero work we do, we’re making hardened daylighting a standard part of our approach. The nuance is just that there are cases– you know, we look at the crash data, and there’s

other treatments in addition to daylighting that are sometimes even more effective. So, we really value the flexibility to use daylighting and/or other approaches based on the situation.

So, we would like to understand how many dollars are going to spent for each fiscal year since you gave us a calculation of how much it will cost. In return, we would like to understand how many intersections are in your budget for this fiscal year. I’ll turn it over back to the Chair, but I would like to come back for a second round of questioning. Thank you.
Okay, great. Council Member Louis followed by Council Member Wong.

Thank you, Chair, and good morning, Commissioner to your whole team. I have four questions, so I’m just going to throw them out, and then hopefully you’ll be able to respond. So, the administration has made significant investments in traffic operations, and my first question targets traffic studies and federal design standards. I wanted to know– there are significant communities that are all going through this, but I wanted to know, despite these significant investments

made by the administration many communities continue to experience year-long waits for traffic studies, signal timing reviews, stop sign requests, and pedestrian safety improvements. I wanted to know how much of– how much this– the increase in funding is dedicated specifically to traffic engineering staff study capacity, and what is the current average timeline from community request to final agency determination for those studies. Also, given that New York City contributes significant local funding towards its transportation network, I wanted to know why is the city continuing to rely so heavily on standards, federal standards specifically that make communities believe that they– communities believe they fail to reflect the realities of dense urban neighborhoods. I wanted to know how is DOT exploring alternatives to methodologies that better account for pedestrian activity, senior population, schools, and houses of worship and transit usage. That's still for traffic studies. And my last question in regards to contractor accountability, utility costs, and cost recovery. I wanted to know– so my constituents frequently raise questions and concerns regarding utility contractor street

restorations that fail shortly after work is completed, leaving residents with deteriorated roadways despite recent construction activity. So, how many summonses or enforcement actions did DOT issue in fiscal year 26 against utilities and contractors for defective street restorations? How much money did the city actually recover through those penalties, corrective work requirements and reimbursements, and is DOT seeking additional resources in the budget to strengthen this enforcement function? Thank you. I know that was a lot.

No, thank you, Council Member. Those are great questions. I’ll just speak briefly to I think one of the points and then maybe let the team chime in on some of them. But regarding federal standards, definitely appreciate that point, and I think, you know, we would agree that cities are very different than let’s say rural areas or even suburban. And we really do seek to maximize our flexibility in how we approach these things. It’s also why we have a great partnership with organizations like NACTO [sic] that advocates for city’s interests. So, I just wanted to mention

that. I think then there was the funding for traffic engineering staff and the utility cars.
So, for traffic operations staff, we already have a robust team that will get signal and other traffic devices. With this budget, we’re adding another 20 people as part of the–
[interposing] Okay.
bus and bike lanes.
And those 20 are dispersed citywide?
They look at the whole entire city. It’s not like they’re just going to focus on each distinct piece. They’re going to continue to move all the pieces of the traffic operation portfolio forward.
Thank you.

Okay. You packed a powerful question, a lot of good stuff in there. So, I think first and foremost, what you’re getting at is how can we be more responsive to communities. People believe they have a problem, and–
[interposing] Correct.

we’re taking too long to look into some of these things like traffic signal studies which we do agree that is taking a long time as well as the ability to then if we find a traffic signal is warranted, to put that in a contract. So, we’re working really hard to staff up in some of these areas, and also to make sure we have more contracting capacity which we should have this coming year. But what I’d like to urge Council Members, as you see an issue, we want to get with you and your constituents on that issue. We have mobile speed camera units, for example. We can put those out if it falls within, you know, our criteria for that. We can look at some other measures for traffic calming. Some things we can do in the short run. We can even look at a longer-term redesign if that’s warranted. But we want to make sure you and your constituents know that’s what we’re here for. We will try to address those needs.
That will be helpful.

And you mentioned MUTCD, this manual for uniform traffic control devices. So that is something that we do need to comply with to retain a federal standard, you know, across the whole country. However, we are being proactive as you mentioned. You mentioned like more pedestrian focus, warrants [sic], and things of that nature.
Right.

We recently worked with the federal government to be able to use micromobility in our studies which is of course something knew, and we were effective at getting that in, and we would want to keep refining as we go forward.
We look forward to that. Thank you. Thank you, Chair.

And we do have some– real quick– inspection information. So the last full fiscal year for fiscal 25 we conducted 474,000 inspections of permitted work out in the streets. 88 percent of those inspections showed that they were in compliance and then they passed basically our inspections.
How many were not in compliance?
That would leave 12 percent.
Okay.
And that could be something like they’re working outside of permitted hours or a street cut was not properly backfilled, something like that.
Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you. Just want to recognize we’ve been joined by Council Member Krishnan, and before we go to Council Member Wong, I just wanted to give a special shout out to the student in the balcony from PSI 155. Thank you so much for being here today. I know you’re from Council Member Rita Joseph’s district who I see back there, but thank you so much for coming to observe how civic participation in city government works. So, thank you. Okay, so Council Member Wong followed by Council Member Epstein.

Okay. Thank you, Chairs. Commissioner Flynn, at the last hearing I was

asking about how can we as the committee, how can DOT improve the safety of pedestrians from e-bike accidents, and unfortunately I got to talk about it again today because yesterday 8:30 there was an e-bike that had a head-on collision with a scooter on Queensboro Bridge and unfortunately both men were killed. I looked at the pictures and I– based upon what I saw, the e-bike involved was a Blade GT2 which has a speed of up to 53 mile per hour. And I asked this before, and here I am again, what can we do as the Finance Committee and what can you do as DOT to enforce speed limits, and why are these high-speed e-scooters be allowed to be on the streets? Please talk about that.

Yeah. Thank you so much for the question, Council Member. And you know, I want to start by saying yesterday’s crash was a tragedy and our hearts are with the victims, their families, and loved ones. You know, I– it’s tough too because pretty recently we were celebrating the opening of the south outer roadway on the bridge that separated pedestrians and cyclists. And you know, to be clear, we do see that as a major step forward in safety for those cycling over the bridge. But

nevertheless, we clearly have work to do. I know the NYPD investigation is ongoing, but based on the facts as we understand them, one of the riders was using a stand-up e-scooter capable of going over 50 miles an hour which is very much illegal in New York City. so, you know, that– I think it really underscores– and we hear it. And there’s a lot of confusion, even myself sometimes. Like, there’s so many different kinds of devices. Some are legal, some are not. Are they pedal-assist? Are they throttle, stand-up, sit-down, all of that different classes? To me, what it underscores is that the highest speed devices are not appropriate for New York City streets. And by in large our laws reflect that. The question is how do we get them off our streets, because again the stand-up scooter involved yesterday, it wasn’t legal to begin with. So, you know, we work closely with NYPD and we have a good partnership, but clearly it underscores that as these devices proliferate, we really have even more work to do to get them off our streets. That’s educating consumers, businesses, but also just confiscating them.

Yes, and if this budget is an issue, please talk to the Finance Chair

of this committee of how can we help, because we just don’t want to see any more of these fatalities, and it’s very unfortunate for we to even talk about this again.
Absolutely. We appreciate that.
Do I have time for one more question? Okay, I’ll do round two. Thank you.
Okay, perfect. Council Member Epstein followed by Council Member Morano on Zoom.

Thank you. Thank you, Chair. I’m going to follow up with the Council Member’s questions around pedestrian safety. I know you said you do a lot of community engagement when you’re making street design changes. How much are you committed to ensuring that the Community Board and local leader’s feedback is taken into consideration when making decisions and changes?
Absolutely. We value the input that we get from communities, from electeds, from Community Boards and it’s one of the important factors that we take into account.

I really do appreciate it. Because if a Community Board says we don’t want to do something, it sounds like DOT should side with the local electeds and the Community Board in their decisions. Is that what I hear from you, Commissioner?
I think at the end of the day, we have an important mission to save New Yorkers’ lives, and–
[interposing] Right.
so we’re balancing all different factors.

Right, exactly. So we’re talking about saving New Yorkers’ lives and pedestrians, and I appreciate you listening to communities when issues come up like that. I know you mentioned expansion of bus pilots, and I really appreciate you wanting to do that. It’s really important to expand those bus pilots. Can you– in lower Manhattan do you– I know we talked about Madison Avenue. I’ve talked to you a lot about the 14A bus. Are there any expansions potentially coming for lower Manhattan at this point?
Around buses specifically?

Yes, bus lanes. You talked speeding up buses. You know, this is something I’ve been working on for many, many years prior to coming to the Council. I’m wondering if you have any proposed projects coming to lower Manhattan.
We will have the faster buses action plan coming out in the coming weeks, and there’ll be a lot of big ideas in there. We're excited to share. We’re excited to work with you and other partners–
[interposing] Yeah.
you know, to basically help flesh out what those projects look like.
Right.
And we’re prioritizing roots like I said earlier based on ridership and bus speeds or things like that. So, I don’t– I’m not sure specifically about Manhattan, but–
[interposing] Sure, sure.
I’m sure we have some ideas there.

Yeah. I would love that, and you know, we talked about the Avenue A bus lane. I’d love to see that expanded as we’ve talked about before. I want to talk about charging infrastructure. We’re talking about to be more environmentally sound, putting publicly available charging infrastructure in place. I’ve been asking DOT for the last 10 years to make one publicly available charging station in lower Manhattan someplace. Can you commit to making publicly available chargers available in lower Manhattan for people who want to convert to electric vehicles?

Well, you know, I’ll start by just reinforcing, you know, absolutely we’re working across with all the levers we have to try to expand EV charging. Starting– you know, with the starting point being that we want to expand options for New Yorkers to walk, bike, and take transit, but we know some folks have to travel by car sometimes, and we certainly want them to be using electric

vehicles in those instances. So, we’re really taking an all of the above approach to EV charging, and that includes on an off street, level two, and fast charging. We’re trying to– one thing we’re doing is trying to prioritize neighborhoods where we see a lot of for-hire vehicle drives live, taxi drivers, things like that, and prioritize charging in those areas. But we’re definitely rolling it out across the city and I can definitely commit to working with you to figure our the best place to put it in–
[interposing] Yeah, I’d love to see at least one in lower Manhattan, and I appreciate your working with me on that. I know I’m out of time. So I’ll come back later, Chair. Thank you.
Council Member Restler followed by Council Member Justin Sanchez. Is he here? Okay, we’ll see if he comes back.

Thank you so much, Chair Lee and Chair Abreu for your leadership of this hearing, and thank you to the DoT team for joining us today. You know, I will say I generally feel that we have leadership at City Hall and leadership in the agency that have the right values

and the right vision. I still think that there are areas where the bureaucracy within the agency is not working well, and I’m really hoping that we’re going to start to see tangible progress on those fronts in the weeks and months to come. So I want to highlight a few of those areas in my questioning today. First up is pedestrian lighting. Last year, we passed a Local Law to require DOT to install pedestrian lighting on 300 commercial corridor blocks every year. The law takes effect January 1st of 2027, so this fiscal year. Has DOT added funding for this to comply with this legislation, and are you confident in your ability to be in compliance in this coming year?

I can just– I’ll start out and then maybe First Deputy Commissioner will want to speak about the ped lighting. Yeah, I just want to underscore in so many of the conversations I’ve had since starting this job, it’s really become clear how important lighting is to New Yorkers and to Council Members and communities. It’s something that people really feel day-to-day. So, it’s something I can assure you I’m very focused on,

street lighting across the board, but maybe you want to speak to the ped lighting specifically.

Yes, and before I mention that, I also want to mention that we do have significant funding in our budget to replace the LEDs around the whole city which will also include a component that will alert us if any given street light is out or needs attention. So, you know, we’re very committed to this area, both keeping up with what we currently have and then making sure we have additional lighting. We are working through with OMB on how we’re going to comply with the Council law.
Just to be clear, there’s now additional funding in the budget to comply with the law at this time?
Well, we did a lot of funding for street lighting, and we’re going to have to work–
[interposing] Do you have funding in the budget to comply with the law? Do you have the funding to comply with the law? It’s just a yes or no question.
We’re in active coordination with OMB and City Hall and all funding needs, and–
[interposing] But you have your Executive Budget. Do you have the funding to be able to comply or not? I just want a yes or no.
We’re in active coordination.
That's not a yes or no. Could you please answer the question?
We have a significant amount of funding for lighting, and we’re evaluating all needs.
Can you comply with the law with the resources you have?
That’s exactly what we’re evaluating, Council Member.
Why can you not answer that question if you know what the funding is that you have in the Executive Budget? It’s just–
[interposing] Council Member, we’re in the planning stages.
Okay.
And as you noted, there’s still more time to comply.

I just– you sense the frustration in my voice, A, because you’re not answering the question, but B, because whenever we have lighting needs across our district, best case scenario is three or four years to address them, and it’s often much longer. We identify issues where DOT says these streets are dark. They’re un– you know, which leads to major safety conditions which undermines how small businesses do in our community, and yet, we see incredible slowness. I mean, not– I’m sure it’s a different portion of DOT, but lighting related. When DOT approves the need for a new traffic light, what’s the average time right now from approval to installation of a new traffic light?
It’s a number of months. We do have–
[interposing] How many?
more contracting capacity coming online.
Do you track that? Do you have a date? Is there a time set for how long it takes once a traffic light is improved to install it? What’s the average time today?
It’s about six months.

Okay. We’re getting estimates of even longer. But you understand how frustrating it is for folks in our community. We go to DOT. We say there’s major safety issues at a corner. There’s crashes at a corner. People are dying at this corner. We finally get a study done. We finally get approval, and then it’s six, eight, nine months before there’s any change on the ground.

No, I hear your frustration absolutely, Council Member, and I– you know, I think I speak for everyone that we have no interest in things taking longer than they should. It’s something we’re very focused on. As First Deputy Commissioner mentioned, some of it is tied up in contracts, and we’re really glad that we’re going to have additional capacity coming online.

So, I just– you know, I’m over time. I didn’t even get to ask about

outdoor dining and the morass that that is, but I just– these– just my opening statement is where I’ll close. I’m confident in the values. I’m confident in the vision. There are components of the bureaucracy and this agency that are not working well, and they need to be addressed, and we need rigorous leadership, strong focus on fixing these issues or we’re not going to see the improvements that we all are committed to seeing in this administration. Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member.
Thank you, Council Member. Selvena Brooks-Powers followed by Council Member Krishnan. Oh, and I’m sorry, we’ve been joined by Council Members Banks and also our Deputy Speaker.

Thank you, Chairs, and thank you, Commissioner and Commissioners for your testimony today. I’m going to ask all my questions at once. I can repeat anything that you need me to thereafter. The Executive Plan includes an additional $16.9 million of city funding in fiscal year 27 for the Bus Action Plan. In 2025, DOT

completed nearly 21 miles of protected bus lanes, short of the 30-mile requirement set by the New York City Streets Plan. With this additional funding in place for fiscal year 27, how many miles of protected bus lane does DOT plan to build in the upcoming fiscal year. This Executive Budget also allocates an additional $3 million for a pothole blitz. We continue to see terrible road conditions in the 31st Council District. Can you share which roads in southeast Queens and the Rockaway peninsula DOT plans to repair with this additional funding? And can DOT provide an update regarding the street lighting along Rockaway Beach Boulevard from Beach 62nd Street to Beach 73rd Street? These lights have been out for months now and cause a major public safety hazard to local residents. And then last, I’m going to pick up on an email exchange that we had with Commissioner Garcia earlier. In my district there are persistent and dangerous pothole conditions at the parking lot entrance of the Rockaway YMCA on Beach 73rd Street. The current state of the entrance is unacceptable. The large potholes pose a significant risk of vehicle damage and potential physical injury to our youth and seniors who rely on the YMCA daily or who just cross

that corridor, because we’ve had a number of crashes at that intersection as well. Could you please confirm if this location is currently on the DOT list for repairs? DOT has also indicated that coordination with DEP is needed to move forward. But we can’t wait any longer. So someone has to take the mantle on this. What is the timeline for this joint repair with DEP? And again, I can repeat anything that needs to be.

Thank you so much, Council Member. I’ll just kind of start at the top here. You asked about the Bus Action Plan and bus mileage. One thing I also want to note is that the mileage is kind of comprised of two pieces. So there’s the physical design we do to create or upgrade bus lanes, bus ways and the street design, and then there’s also the automated camera enforcement from MTA. So you mentioned the mileage from last year. So, you know, our bus program for this year, it’s in active development so I don’t have an exact number, but what I can say is that it’s a historic level of investment that we’re seeing starting in July, and therefore we expecting a historic level of output this year, significantly

exceeding past years when it comes to mileage and even more in future years in terms of output. I think next you asked about pothole blitz and just generally paving conditions in southeast Queens.

I noted the location that you just provided at the entrance to the parking lot, so we will get out there in the next 24 to 48 hours. We will address that. You asked about pothole repair as the result of the funding. The funding is paying for all of those pothole blitz that we had where we addressed over 100,000 pothole conditions, but at this moment in terms of 311 input for potholes, we have only a few hundred. We can keep up with potholes now that we’ve gotten through the worst of it. So, in general for you or for the whole Council, for the public, any potholes let us know. Call them into 311. You just call us any time and we will have them addressed very quickly. You also mentioned, I think, Auverne by the Sea [sic] the lighting issue, Council Member?
Yes. We've been working on that since– as you know, since last year.

Correct. Our Borough Commissioner updated me a few days ago that we’re doing everything we can to help the developer and HPD understand exactly what light fixtures need to get installed to the extent that we are even going to provide one that they can use, and then they can purchase more to have them all rectified and replaced.

I think it’s pretty alarming how long it’s taking with coordination with sister agencies with something that’s a public safety matter. Like, literally with lighting being completely out and for such a duration of time.
Okay, we are 100 percent available to assist in any way. Those streets don’t belong to us–
[interposing] No, they belong to
[inaudible] under our jurisdiction–

[interposing] But there needs to be greater coordination because DOT is still responsible for the

conditions of the streets. I understand because of the urban development that took place it’s under HPD right now, but there has to be coordination. There can’t continue to be finger pointing between the agencies.

No, I understand and I agree. So we are providing actually several light poles to them in order to really help them understand what has to happen. We’ll be on the ground with them at any moment that they need us out there to help figure out the problem.
Great. Thank you.
Thank you.
Council Member Krishnan followed by Council Member Banks.

Thank you so much, Chairs. Good to see you all, Commissioner, First Deputy Commissioner, all DOT team. I just had a few questions. So, one– and I apologize if this came up before, too, but as you all know, we’ve been very close partners working together along our Open Street program across the city, especially in Jackson Heights where we’ve got the most successful one in my

non-biased opinion. But I just want to get a sense of what funding have you allocated for the program, and how are you envisioning– for the program overall across the city– and how are you envisioning prioritizing Open Streets with the new budget?

Thank you, Council Member. Yeah, so we’re really glad that thanks to the $6.4 million that we added to the budget, we’re able to keep the baseline for the Open Streets. Also excited that we have– I guess last week we announced the launch of the Open Streets season, and we already over 150 initial locations which is about 20 percent more than where we were at this point last year, and still more to come. So, that’s great. Yeah, so our intention is really to keep the program growing and actually to keep kind of innovating and thinking across the board with all of our open space and public realm initiatives, how we can support communities, how we can build in even better structures from operations and maintenance standpoint.

Great. I’m glad to hear. I’m glad that’s a priority, too. And I wanted to mention one thing with that as well, and I

appreciate you and your team, Commissioner, and the Deputy Mayor coming out to visit our Open Street. As you know, and Council Member Wong mentioned this too, it was very, very tragic to read the story about what happened on the Queensboro Bridge with the e-bike and our scooter and our cyclist my real, real concern and you all know it well too is that we can have similar– we’ve had narrow misses or children hit by mopeds on our Open Street on 34th Avenue which is very successful, and I’m very concerned about this conflict between mopeds that are taking over and creating highway there and a pedestrian space. And so what I’d love to keep working on together is we really need to look at Northern Boulevard as a solution for mopeds which are Class Three motor vehicles. They belong with cars, not with people. And I think to get the Open Street to be successful, we need to really solve this moped situation in an effective way, and that involves looking at other places for micromobility uses and lanes. And I’d hope to be able to work with you all on doing so.

Thank you, Council Member. I agree that, you know, the– as we’ve seen more proliferation of these two-wheel devices, and

again, some are classified as e-bikes. Some like you mentioned are actually– should be in the road with motor vehicles. This is really an area of focus for us and we know it’s very urgent for a lot of New Yorkers as well. So, we’re always happy to look at big ideas and figure out how to solve these things.

Well, I look forward to that work together, too, on northern and south. And my last question is on Northern Boulevard, there’s– we have a bus lane now which has been very effective and we appreciate your work on that too. The biggest problem we’re seeing, and I see it myself, is on the weekends, at night time, so many cars are double-parked and use it as parking lot, basically and it’s down miles in front of all the bars there, too.
